# Data sources

## Links and how to reproduce the data selection

MOST ?? files are downloaded from the World Bank Open Data portal. The World Bank only redistributes the health and behaviour indicators, which are produced by the WHO. To reproduce the selection:

| Variable | Producer | Indicator page | Local file |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Out-of-pocket health expenditure (% of current health expenditure) | WHO GHED, via World Bank | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.XPD.OOPC.CH.ZS> | `data/out_of_pocket.csv` |
| Alcohol consumption per capita (litres of pure alcohol, 15+) | WHO GHO, via World Bank | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.ALC.PCAP.LI> | `data/alcohol.csv` |
| Tobacco use (smoking prevalence) | WHO GHO, via World Bank | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SH.PRV.SMOK> | `data/tobacco.csv` |
| GDP per capita, PPP (constant international \$) | World Bank (ICP / WDI) | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD> | `data/gdp.csv` |
| Life expectancy at birth, total (years) | World Bank (WDI) | <https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.LE00.IN> | `data/life_expectancy.csv` |

## Short description of the sources

Our data come mainly from datasets of the World Health Organization (WHO) that are redistributed by the World Bank.

**Out-of-pocket expenditure.** The share of out-of-pocket spending in current health expenditure comes from the WHO Global Health Expenditure Database (GHED), updated on 12 December 2025. It is built on the System of Health Accounts (SHA 2011) framework. Out-of-pocket payments are the health expenditures paid directly by households at the time they receive care. The WHO presents this share as a key indicator of financial protection: the higher it is, the less the population is protected against the cost of care. This is our main explanatory variable.

**Alcohol.** Alcohol consumption per capita comes from the WHO Global Health Observatory (GHO). It is the sum of the recorded consumption (three-year average) and an estimate of the unrecorded consumption, for people aged 15 and over, in litres of pure alcohol. The World Bank redistributes it under the code SH.ALC.PCAP.LI.

**Tobacco.** The tobacco indicator (SH.PRV.SMOK) also comes from the WHO GHO and is published under a CC BY 4.0 licence. The WHO estimates cover 2000 to 2024 with projections up to 2030. Projections are not observations, so we cut the series and keep the years up to 2024.

Alcohol and tobacco are used as proxies of risky behaviours, which is the way we define moral hazard (behaviours adopted *before* illness occurs). This is a limitation: they are national averages and they only capture part of risky behaviours.

**GDP per capita.** It is measured in purchasing power parity, in constant international dollars, and comes from the International Comparison Program database through the World Development Indicators (WDI). The base year of prices changes between WDI versions (2011, 2017 or 2021), so all the files must come from the same download session. GDP is a control variable, because income influences both access to care and behaviours.

**Life expectancy.** The WDI indicator "Life expectancy at birth, total (years)" is our main target variable, as an overall measure of the health of a population.

# Loading the raw files

The World Bank CSV files have 4 lines of metadata before the header, and one column per year (wide format).

```{r}
#| label: load-raw
files <- tribble(
  ~id,             ~file,                        ~label,
  "out_of_pocket", "data/out_of_pocket.csv",     "Out-of-pocket expenditure",
  "alcohol",       "data/alcohol.csv",           "Alcohol consumption",
  "tobacco",       "data/tobacco.csv",           "Tobacco use",
  "gdp",           "data/gdp.csv",               "GDP per capita (PPP)",
  "life_exp",      "data/life_expectancy.csv",   "Life expectancy at birth"
)

raw <- files$file |>
  map(\(f) read_csv(f, skip = 4, show_col_types = FALSE)) |>
  set_names(files$id)
```

## One table per data file

All the numbers below are computed from the files.

```{r}
#| label: file-tables
#| results: asis
for (i in seq_len(nrow(files))) {
  df <- raw[[i]]
  year_cols <- grep("^[0-9]{4}$", names(df), value = TRUE)
  values <- as.matrix(df[year_cols])
  info <- tibble(
    Item = c("File", "Number of rows (countries and aggregates)",
             "Number of columns", "Number of year columns",
             "First year", "Last year",
             "Share of missing values in year columns"),
    Value = c(files$file[i], nrow(df), ncol(df), length(year_cols),
              min(year_cols), max(year_cols),
              sprintf("%.1f %%", 100 * mean(is.na(values))))
  )
  cat("\n\n**", files$label[i], "**\n\n", sep = "")
  print(kable(info, align = c("l", "r")))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

## Most important variables

| Variable | Description |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `country`, `iso3` | Name and ISO 3166 alpha-3 code of the country. They identify the statistical unit and are the first key used to join the files. |
| `year` | Calendar year of the observation. With `iso3`, it forms the key of our country-year panel. |
| `life_exp` | Life expectancy at birth in years. |
| `oop_share` | Out-of-pocket expenditure as a percentage of current health expenditure. High values mean a weak financial protection. Main explanatory variable. |
| `alcohol` | Alcohol consumption per capita (litres of pure alcohol, population 15+, recorded and unrecorded). Proxy of risky behaviour. |
| `tobacco` | Prevalence of tobacco smoking. Proxy of risky behaviour. |
| `gdp_pc` | GDP per capita in PPP, constant international dollars. Control variable for the level of wealth. |

# Joining and cleaning

We applied the following steps:

1.  **Reshaping.** Each file is converted from wide format (one column per year) to long format (one row per country and year).
2.  **Period.** We keep the years 2000 to 2024. This removes the years without data and excludes the WHO projections for tobacco (2025 to 2030). NOT SURE FOR NOW
3.  **Joining.** The five tables are joined by country code and year with a full join, so that no observation is lost at this stage.
4.  **Aggregates.** The World Bank files contain regions and income groups (World, Euro area, etc.). They are not countries, so they are removed by keeping only the codes recognised as countries by the `countrycode` package.
5.  **Missing values.** We count them for each variable. The analysis sample keeps only the country-years where the variables are all observed.

```{r}
#| label: clean-join
to_long <- function(df, name) {
  df |>
    select(country = `Country Name`, iso3 = `Country Code`,
           matches("^[0-9]{4}$")) |>
    pivot_longer(-c(country, iso3), names_to = "year", values_to = name) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>
    filter(year >= 2000, year <= 2024)
}

panel_all <- list(
  to_long(raw$out_of_pocket, "oop_share"),
  to_long(raw$alcohol,       "alcohol"),
  to_long(raw$tobacco,       "tobacco"),
  to_long(raw$gdp,           "gdp_pc"),
  to_long(raw$life_exp,      "life_exp")
) |>
  reduce(full_join, by = c("country", "iso3", "year"))

panel <- panel_all |>
  filter(!is.na(countrycode(iso3, "iso3c", "country.name", warn = FALSE)))

panel_complete <- panel |> drop_na()
```

After joining, the table has `r nrow(panel_all)` rows. Once the aggregates are removed, there are `r nrow(panel)` rows for `r n_distinct(panel$iso3)` countries. The complete sample, without any missing value, has `r nrow(panel_complete)` rows for `r n_distinct(panel_complete$iso3)` countries.

```{r}
#| label: missing
panel |>
  summarise(across(c(oop_share, alcohol, tobacco, gdp_pc, life_exp),
                   \(x) sprintf("%.1f %%", 100 * mean(is.na(x))))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable",
               values_to = "Share of missing values") |>
  kable(align = c("l", "r"))
```

# Research question

**To what extent does the reduction in households' direct out-of-pocket health expenditure influence individual health behaviours, and to what extent can it foster the emergence of moral hazard?**

In most developed countries, health care is largely financed through public spending or collective insurance. The expected effect is positive: when access to care no longer depends on income, prevention, screening and treatment improve, and life expectancy rises. By contrast, countries where out-of-pocket spending (the share paid directly by the patient) is high experience more forgone care and greater health inequalities. A first part of our work is therefore to check whether a lower out-of-pocket share is associated with a higher life expectancy.

However, when people no longer bear the full cost of their choices, they may be tempted to behave more recklessly: smoking more, drinking, neglecting prevention. This is the classical argument of moral hazard. In our analysis, moral hazard refers only to risky behaviours adopted *before* illness occurs, which is different from the excess use of care once a person is ill. We use alcohol consumption and tobacco use as proxies of these behaviours. This choice has limits, since these two indicators do not cover all risky behaviours (diet, physical activity, prevention, screening), but they are available for many countries over a long period.

The difficulty is that health behaviours also depend on education, income, culture, religion and public prevention policies (taxes on tobacco and alcohol, advertising bans, awareness campaigns). Isolating the specific effect of insurance coverage is therefore hard. A country with low out-of-pocket spending is often a rich country, with a high level of education and strong prevention policies, which can hide or reverse a possible moral hazard effect. This is why we include GDP per capita as a control, and why we plan to test additional variables such as education or road traffic deaths.

The question is thus whether moral hazard is a real and measurable phenomenon, or rather a theoretical risk whose magnitude remains limited compared with the benefits of a well-funded health system. We can state two working hypotheses:

-   **H1.** A lower out-of-pocket share is associated with a higher life expectancy, even after controlling for GDP per capita.
-   **H2.** A lower out-of-pocket share is associated with higher alcohol consumption and tobacco use (moral hazard), but the effect is small compared with the gain in life expectancy.

Methodologically, we will carry out a longitudinal study. Since the studies are conducted at the country level and there are not enough countries in the world to reach 1000 units, we use data by year: each observation is a country in a given year. This gives a panel of several thousand observations and allows us to follow the same country over time, for instance with country fixed effects, to compare a country with itself rather than with very different countries.

The main limitation of the project is that we only have national averages. A relation observed between countries does not necessarily hold for individuals (ecological fallacy), so we cannot draw firm conclusions about individual behaviours. Our results will describe associations and not proven causal effects.

# Target variable: life expectancy

Life expectancy at birth is our target variable. The first graph shows its distribution over all the country-years, the second one its evolution over time.

```{r}
#| label: fig-target-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of life expectancy at birth (all countries and years)"
panel |>
  filter(!is.na(life_exp)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = life_exp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Life expectancy at birth (years)", y = "Number of country-years") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-target-time
#| fig-cap: "Evolution of life expectancy: median and interquartile range across countries"
panel |>
  filter(!is.na(life_exp)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(median = median(life_exp),
            q1 = quantile(life_exp, 0.25),
            q3 = quantile(life_exp, 0.75)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q1, ymax = q3), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

A first look at the relation with our main explanatory variable (the complete sample is used):

```{r}
#| label: fig-target-oop
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy and out-of-pocket share, all country-years with complete data"
panel_complete |>
  ggplot(aes(x = oop_share, y = life_exp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Out-of-pocket expenditure (% of current health expenditure)",
       y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)") +
  theme_minimal()
```
